subject: physics
question_text: Describe the behaviour of a wire under gradually increasing load.

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2017 (Q17), March 2020 (Q17), March 2024 (Q18) and March 2025 (Q16) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section B, 4 marks each time. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: Hooke's law (stress ∝ strain) holds only up to the proportional limit; the elastic limit is the last point of full recovery and a permanent set remains beyond it; the yield point begins the plastic region, where strain grows for little added stress; the wire narrows at one place before it breaks at the fracture point.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The stress–strain curve
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. The question asks for a description, so this is a study drawing that holds the four named points in the right order.
steps.why: Every named point in the answer sits on this one curve, so drawing it first keeps P, E, Y and F in the order the description needs.
common_mistakes: Drawing strain up the vertical axis. Stress goes up the vertical axis and strain along the horizontal one.
Marking the fracture point at the highest point of the curve. The highest point comes first, then the wire narrows and breaks.

recall.must_convey: That the answer is built on the stress-strain curve, with P, E, Y and F marked along it in that order.
accept: mark P, E, Y and F on the graph
stress on the y axis and strain on the x axis
reject: stress is proportional to strain up to P

steps.memory_tip: Four points in order along the curve: P, then E, then Y, then F.

steps.label: The proportional region
lines: The wire is loaded a little at a time and the
extension is measured at each load.
At first the graph is a straight line through
the origin: stress is proportional to strain.
The stress at the end of this straight part
is the proportional limit, P.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the straight part as Hooke's law and name P as the proportional limit.
steps.why: Hooke's law is a law of the straight part only. The wire keeps stretching after P, but no longer in proportion to the load.
common_mistakes: Saying Hooke's law holds up to the breaking point. It holds only up to the proportional limit.
Saying the wire is not elastic after P. It is still elastic between P and E; it is only no longer proportional.

recall.must_convey: That the first part of the graph is a straight line through the origin where stress is proportional to strain, ending at the proportional limit P.
reject: a permanent set is left in the wire

steps.memory_tip: Straight line means Hooke's law. P is the point where the line stops being straight.

steps.label: Elastic limit and yield point
lines: Just past P the graph bends, but the wire
still returns to its original length when the
load is removed. The stress at the last point
of full recovery is the elastic limit, E.
Beyond E the wire does not return fully. A
permanent set is left in the wire.
At the yield point Y the wire stretches a lot
for very little added stress. This is the
plastic region.
steps.margin_note: Two marks here. One for the elastic limit and the permanent set, one for the yield point and the plastic region.
steps.why: The elastic limit and the yield point are two different points that sit close together on the graph. E is about recovery; Y is about strain growing fast for almost no added stress.
common_mistakes: Treating the elastic limit and the yield point as the same point. E is where full recovery ends; Y is where the strain starts growing fast.
Saying the wire returns to its original length after E. Past E a permanent set stays in the wire.

recall.must_convey: That E is the elastic limit, the last point of full recovery, that a permanent set remains beyond it, and that at the yield point Y the strain grows for little added stress.
accept: a permanent set is left in the wire
at the yield point strain grows for little stress

steps.memory_tip: E is the last point of full recovery. Past E a permanent set stays in the wire.

steps.label: The fracture point
lines: In the plastic region the wire keeps
stretching under an almost steady load. The
stress reaches a maximum, the wire narrows at
one place, and at the fracture point F it
breaks.

lines.text: Elastic up to E, plastic after Y, breaks at F

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Say that the wire narrows at one place first and then breaks at F.
steps.why: The load at F is often smaller than the largest load the wire carried, because the wire has thinned at one place and the same load now acts on a smaller area.
common_mistakes: Saying the wire breaks at the point of maximum stress. It thins at one place first and breaks a little after that point.
Leaving F unnamed. The question is a list of named points, and F is one of them.

recall.must_convey: That the stress reaches a maximum, the wire narrows at one place, and it breaks at the fracture point F.
accept: the wire narrows and then breaks

steps.memory_tip: The wire thins at one place first, then breaks, so F comes after the highest point.

insider_note: Four marks for four named points. An answer that describes the stretching without naming P, E, Y and F collects one or two.
